options.why: Assumed any net containing triangles must be a pyramid; a pyramid has one base with triangles meeting at an apex, not two separate triangular ends.
Named the solid from the three rectangles only and ignored the two triangular end faces.
Took a rectangle as the base and read the two triangles as sloping faces rising to an apex, ignoring that three rectangles form the sides.

questions.solution_text:
The net has two identical triangular ends joined by three rectangles.
The triangle edges match the rectangle widths, and the arrangement folds without overlap or gaps.
The solid is a triangular prism.

options.why: Treated all the faces as equal squares, although the side faces are rectangles twice as long as they are wide.
Mistook the square ends for a pyramid base, although the side faces are rectangles rather than triangles meeting at an apex.
Named triangular ends even though both end faces are squares.

questions.solution_text:
The two end faces are identical squares. The four rectangular side faces have widths matching the square edges.
The arrangement folds without overlap or gaps into a square prism.

options.why: Assumed four equal sides make a square, ignoring that the end faces have sloping sides and no right angles.
Treated the end faces as having only one pair of parallel sides, although each rhombus has two pairs.
Named the solid from its rectangular side faces and ignored the rhombus-shaped ends.

questions.solution_text:
Each end face is a rhombus: its four sides are equal and its opposite sides are parallel.
The rectangle widths match those sides, and the strip folds around the two ends without overlap or gaps.
The solid is a rhombic prism.
